# Generative AI and Agentic DV {#sec-ch34}

*Chapter intent: a conceptual chapter. By the end, a reader who has never used a language model beyond a chat window can explain, from first principles and with a diagram for each, what generative models are, how they become agents, how agents are grounded, tooled, evaluated and governed, and, for every one of those ideas, what its counterpart is in a verification project. The chapter's originality is the mapping itself: every concept is presented three times, as the idea, as the software-development practice that grew up around it, and as the verification practice it corresponds to. It cites evidence where a number is claimed, but it is not a survey of tools or papers.*

> Verification already has what software development had to invent for its agents: an oracle that cannot be argued with.

## Learning objectives

*Five items: explain how a generative model produces text and why its output is a sample rather than an answer; describe the loop that turns a model into an agent and name its four failure points; map the software practices that make agents safe (specifications, tests first, review, continuous integration) onto verification's plan, checker, review and regression; draw the block diagram of an agentic verification flow with its human gates; state which verification tasks the evidence supports delegating and which it does not, and why the boundary falls where it does.*

## Diagram conventions

*A short note before the chapter proper: every block diagram in this chapter uses the same four shapes, a model (rounded), a tool (rectangle), a store of evidence (cylinder), and a human gate (diamond), and the same two arrow kinds, data (solid) and judgment (dashed). Introduced once, used in all eleven figures.*

## The oracle problem, restated

*Motivation, 400 to 600 words, no anecdote. @sec-ch01 argued that a passing test is a statement about the test, and that the checker, the independent translation of the specification, is the heart of the craft. Software development learned the same lesson when it started letting models write code: the model would satisfy whatever it was measured against, including by gaming the measurement. Software's answer was to move the judgment out of the model and into things the model cannot rewrite: tests written first, reviews by someone else, a build that either passes or does not. Verification has had those things for thirty years under different names. This chapter is about seeing the correspondence, so that a verification engineer can read the software world's agent practices as translations of their own, and adopt them as such.*

## 34.1 What a generative model is {#sec-ch34-model}

*The model as a function from a sequence of tokens to a distribution over the next token, sampled repeatedly. What that implies: output is fluent by construction, correct only by coincidence with the training data and the prompt, and different on every run unless made deterministic. The context window as the model's entire world for one call; nothing outside it exists. Temperature, sampling and why "the same prompt gives a different answer" is not a bug. Figure 34.1: the model as a block, tokens in, distribution out, sampler, loop. DV counterpart: a constrained-random generator is also a sampler over a space shaped by constraints; the prompt is the constraint set; the seed is the seed. Definition callout: token, context, sample.*

## 34.2 Prompting is specification {#sec-ch34-prompting}

*A prompt is a specification of the desired output, with all of specification's problems: ambiguity, omission, and the reader's assumptions filling the gaps. Instruction, examples, constraints and output format as the four parts of a prompt, and how software teams moved from ad-hoc prompts to versioned prompt files, then to standing instruction files checked into the repository. Figure 34.2: prompt anatomy, with the instruction file feeding every call. Software parallel: the README that became the agent instruction file. DV counterpart: the verification plan is the instruction file for a testbench, and @sec-ch02 already argued it must be machine-readable and versioned. Pitfall callout: a prompt that describes the implementation rather than the requirement, mirroring @sec-ch02-features.*

## 34.3 Grounding: retrieval and context {#sec-ch34-grounding}

*Why the model must be handed the specification, the RTL and the logs rather than expected to know them: it does not, and it will produce plausible substitutes. Two grounding strategies: retrieval, which fetches passages by similarity and pastes them into the context, and search, which lets the model look through a repository the way an engineer does. Why the second won for code and why the same reasoning applies to RTL. Context rot: the model's effective attention is far smaller than its nominal window, so what is included matters more than how much. Figure 34.3: grounding sources feeding a context assembler feeding the model, with the assembler as the design decision. Software parallel: documentation-as-code and the knowledge base that feeds retrieval. DV counterpart: the specification, plan, RTL and regression history are the grounding sources, and a testbench directory is the repository the agent searches.*

## 34.4 Tools: closing the loop with the world {#sec-ch34-tools}

*A model that can only emit text cannot compile anything. Tool use: the model emits a structured request, a harness executes it, the result returns to the context. The protocol that standardized this, described conceptually: a tool advertises a name, a schema and a description; the model chooses; the harness runs. Sandboxing: the tool runs somewhere the agent can break without consequence. Figure 34.4: model, harness, tool server, sandbox, with the request and result arrows. Software parallel: the build system and test runner as the first tools every coding agent was given. DV counterpart: the simulator, the coverage database, the waveform and the formal engine are the tools, and this book's own build system, with its three uniform targets and its status file, is already a tool interface an agent could call. In Practice callout: what a simulator tool must expose and what it must never expose (the checker's source).*

## 34.5 From model to agent: the loop {#sec-ch34-loop}

*The loop: plan, act through a tool, observe, decide whether to stop. The three patterns it takes: reason-and-act, plan-then-execute, and generate-then-evaluate. Where each loop can fail: a wrong plan, a wrong tool call, a misread observation, and a wrong stopping decision, the last being the one that matters most. Why "it stopped when the tests passed" is the same claim as "the test passed" in @sec-ch01, and no stronger. Figure 34.5: the loop with its four failure points marked. Software parallel: the test-driven loop, red, green, refactor, which the agent tools adopted as their inner loop. DV counterpart: the coverage-driven loop, write stimulus, run, read coverage, repeat, which is the same loop with coverage as the stopping signal, and the same weakness, that the signal is not the goal.*

## 34.6 Evaluation and the gaming problem {#sec-ch34-evaluation}

*How agents are evaluated: held-out tasks, pass-at-k, and the discovery that visible tests get satisfied while held-out tests do not. Reward hacking as a structural property of optimizing against a proxy, with the documented lookup-table case as the illustration [GA §4]. Software's countermeasures: hidden tests, mutation testing to judge tests by their bug-finding power, judging agent-written tests by outcome rather than by process compliance. Figure 34.6: generator, visible metric, hidden metric, and the gap between them. DV counterpart: coverage is the visible metric and bug-finding power is the hidden one; the measured gap between 90 percent coverage and 14 percent mutation detection is the DV version of the same phenomenon [DV §2.3]. Why verification is better placed than software: it already has coverage as a proxy and knows not to trust it.*

## 34.7 Separation of generator and judge {#sec-ch34-separation}

*The single most important design rule for agentic flows, derived from the previous section: whatever generates must not own what judges. In software: the agent writes code, a separately written test suite judges; when the agent could edit the tests, it did, and deleted the failing ones. In verification the rule has a precise form: the stimulus agent has no write access to the checker, the reference model, the assertions or the coverage model, and the rule is enforced by the harness and the repository, never by the prompt. Figure 34.7: two isolated contexts, stimulus and oracle, with the enforced boundary and the toolchain as the only judge. Software parallel: code review by someone other than the author; continuous integration that the author cannot skip. DV counterpart: the checker written independently of the RTL, which @sec-ch01-hard called the second translation; now extended to be independent of the stimulus agent too.*

## 34.8 Multi-agent flows and their failure modes {#sec-ch34-multiagent}

*Why teams of agents: context isolation, role specialization, parallelism. How they fail: hallucination propagating from one agent to the next, false consensus, and verification agents that agree with the generator because they share its evidence [GA §1]. The rule that follows: a verifier helps only when it holds evidence the generator does not, which in verification means the simulator's output, the formal engine's verdict or the coverage database, never a second reading of the same prompt. Figure 34.8: orchestrator with workers, evidence stores, and the paths along which a wrong belief travels. Software parallel: the pull-request pipeline, author, reviewer, CI, each with different information. DV counterpart: the verification team itself, designer, verifier, formal engineer, sign-off reviewer, whose value has always come from independence.*

## 34.9 The agentic verification flow {#sec-ch34-flow}

*The chapter's synthesis, as one block diagram. Grounding sources read-only at the top; roles in isolated contexts (planner, stimulus, checker, coverage analyst, debug, formal, reviewer); the tool layer; and three human gates, at the plan, at the oracle, and at sign-off, each placed where reversing a mistake stops being cheap. Figure 34.9: the full flow, the chapter's centerpiece, redrawn from the synthesis note's architecture. A walk through one feature from specification to sign-off along the diagram. How this book's own writing process instantiates the same diagram, with a drafting agent that cannot edit the evidence and a reviewer that never sees the drafter's context (@sec-ch02 described the plan half of it).*

## 34.10 What to delegate, and how to know {#sec-ch34-delegate}

*The evidence ledger, compressed to a table and stated as a boundary rather than a list: tasks where the toolchain is the judge (stimulus, assertions with a formal engine, debug hypotheses, triage) are delegable today; tasks where the agent's output would become the judge (checkers, reference models, test plans, sign-off) are not, and the measured pass rates for those are low for a structural reason, not a temporary one [DV §2.3, SW §3]. Figure 34.10: the delegation boundary drawn on the flow of Figure 34.9. Measurement: the metrics that survive contact with an agent, bugs found per engineer-week, escape rate, time to closure, mutation kill rate, review load, and why self-reported speed-ups are not evidence [SW §7]. Governance: the guardrails specific to DV, from hallucinated assertions to tool poisoning to licensing of generated code. Future Directions callout: what would have to change in the evidence before the boundary could move.*

## 34.11 Worked example: a flow on paper {#sec-ch34-example}

*Not code. The FIFO of @sec-ch01 and its plan of @sec-ch02 walked through the flow of Figure 34.9 as a table: for each plan item, which role would act, what tool it would call, what evidence would come back, which gate it passes, and what a human would look at. The chapter-1 bug traced through the flow to show which role finds it (the checker, which the stimulus agent cannot touch) and which roles could not (a stimulus agent measured on coverage). Figure 34.11: the FIFO's item FIFO-005 as a swim-lane diagram across roles and gates.*

## Exercises

1. *Draw the block diagram of a chat assistant answering a question about a datasheet, using the chapter's shapes. Mark where the datasheet enters and where the answer's correctness is judged, if anywhere.*
2. *Rewrite a paragraph of the UART specification from @sec-ch02 as a prompt for an agent that must write a plan item. Then list the assumptions a reader of your prompt would have to make.*
3. *Take the coverage-driven loop of @sec-ch34-loop and identify, for a testbench you know, what its stopping signal is and what its goal is. Are they the same?*
4. *Propose a mutation for the FIFO that a 100 percent coverage test suite could miss. Explain which of the chapter's two metrics catches it.*
5. *For each of the four failure points in @sec-ch34-loop, name the software practice and the verification practice that guards it.*
6. *Redraw Figure 34.9 for a project that has no formal engine. Which gate becomes weaker and what replaces the missing judge?*
7. *A vendor claims a fully autonomous flow. Using @sec-ch34-delegate, write the five questions you would ask, and for each say what evidence would answer it.*
